title: One Set can't rule them all!
description: Should every agent go through the same approval process?
series: Who’s in Control When Everyone Can Build a Copilot?
bodyHtml:
Someone builds an agent to help find documents.

An HR team creates an agent that answers questions about holidays and company policies.

Another agent can update employee records or request time off.

All three are agents. But should they follow the same rules?

Probably not.

The risks are different, so it makes sense to look at what each agent can actually do.

Start with what the agent can do

Before deciding which controls an agent needs, I would start with two questions:

What can it access, and what can it change?

Microsoft describes a three-zone governance approach for Copilot Studio:

  • Citizen Development: Personal productivity and smaller team solutions, with safe defaults.

  • Partnered Development: Agents used by teams or departments, with IT support and review.

  • Professional Development: Business-critical solutions that need stronger controls, testing and release processes.

These zones help organisations decide how much governance different agents need.

They are a recommended approach, not three built-in settings you can simply switch on.



Three agents, three different needs

Agent 1: Finding documents

You create an agent that helps you find information in your own work documents.

Only you use it. It can read information you already have access to, but it cannot change anything.

Basic access and sharing controls may be enough.

Agent 2: Helping colleagues

Your HR team creates an agent that answers common questions about holidays, sick leave and company policies.

Everyone in the company can use it.

Now it becomes important to check whether the answers are correct, which documents the agent uses and who keeps that information up to date.

Agent 3: Updating information

Your HR agent gets a new feature. Employees can now use it to request time off, and the agent can update the HR system.

That's a bigger change.

What happens if it books the wrong dates? Can someone request leave for another employee? What if the HR system is unavailable?

This agent needs additional checks before people start using it.

All three are agents, but the risks are different.

And that's the idea behind the three governance zones. The controls should match what an agent can access, what it can change and what could happen if something goes wrong.

When should you review an agent again?

Look at the HR agent from the previous example.

At first, it only answers questions about company policies.

Later, someone connects it to the HR system so employees can request time off.

The agent might look exactly the same to the employee, but behind the scenes, quite a lot has changed.

It now has access to another system and can change information.

That should be a reason to review its permissions, testing and approval process.

The same applies when an agent gets access to sensitive documents or becomes available to more people.

An agent doesn't automatically need to move to another zone every time something changes. But its controls should still match what it can do.

And that raises another question.

Do makers know when their agent needs additional approval?

If someone wants to share their personal agent with the entire department, there should be a clear process explaining what's allowed and what needs reviewing.

Otherwise, people may only discover the rules when something gets blocked.

Try this with one of your agents

Pick an agent you've built or currently manage.

Ask yourself:

  1. Who can use it?

  2. What information can it access?

  3. Can it change anything?

  4. What happens if it makes a mistake?

  5. Who is responsible for it?

Think about the HR agent again.

When it only answered questions, checking the documents and access might have been enough.

Once it could update the HR system, additional testing and permissions became important.

Would you still give both versions the same level of access and controls?

One thing to keep in mind

Assigning an agent to a governance zone doesn't automatically make it secure.

You still need to configure the actual controls, including sharing, authentication, connectors, data policies and environment access.

And those controls differ between Microsoft Copilot, Agent Builder and Copilot Studio.

The three-zone model is a useful starting point, but the actual configuration is what counts.

What's next?

So far, we've looked at who can use an agent and what it can do.

But there's another question worth exploring.

What happens when an agent can find documents that people probably shouldn't have access to in the first place?

That's what I want to look at in the next episode.

Question: Do you already use different levels of governance for your agents, or does everything go through the same approval process?
